# Tic disorders

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Movement disorders > Tic disorders*

[Original Article Link](/library/sP0tTT)

---

## Summary

<u>Tic</u> disorders are neurological conditions characterized by sudden and rapid movements and/or vocalizations. Primary <u>tic</u> disorders begin in childhood and include <u>Tourette syndrome</u>, <u>persistent (chronic) motor or vocal tic disorder</u>, and <u>provisional tic disorder</u>. Primary <u>tic</u> disorders are often associated with other conditions, including <u>attention deficit hyperactivity disorder</u> (<u>ADHD</u>) and <u>obsessive-compulsive disorder</u> (<u>OCD</u>). The diagnosis is clinical and confirmed using <u>DSM-5-TR</u> diagnostic criteria. The degree of functional impairment should be determined to guide management. Patients without functional impairment may be managed expectantly. <u>Comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics</u> (<u>CBIT</u>) is recommended for all patients with functional impairment. Depending on the response to <u>CBIT</u>, comorbidities, and the severity of symptoms, additional treatment options may be considered, including pharmacological treatment (e.g., <u>alpha-2 receptor agonists</u>, <u>dopamine antagonists</u>) and advanced treatments (e.g., <u>botulinum toxin</u> injection, <u>deep brain stimulation</u>).

---

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)

* Age of onset: usually 4–6 years of age (<u>tics</u> are most severe between 10–12 years of age and then decline during <u>adolescence</u>) [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Hypothesized to be a combination of environmental, social, psychological, and genetic factors

* Associated conditions

* <u>ADHD</u> and/or <u>OCD</u> (most common)

* <u>Learning</u> disabilities

* <u>Sleep disorders</u>

* <u>Conduct disorder</u> and <u>oppositional defiant disorder</u>

* Mood and <u>anxiety disorders</u>

---

## Clinical features

* Tic: sudden and rapid movements or vocalizations that are intermittent, nonrhythmic, and without any recognizable purpose [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)[[2]](/library/06dejI0)

* Usually involuntary but may be temporarily suppressible

* Premonitory urge: An urge or sensation preceding the <u>tic</u> is relieved by its onset.

* Exacerbated by factors such as fatigue and excitement [[2]](/library/06dejI0)

* <u>Tic</u> types [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)

* Simple <u>tic</u>: typically brief, involving few muscles or sounds

* Complex <u>tic</u>: typically longer, coordinated combinations of movements or sounds





| <br>Common features of vocal and motor <u>tics</u> [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Simple | Complex |
| Vocal <u>tics</u> | <br><br>* Throat clearing<br><br>* <u>Grunting</u><br><br>* Lip smacking<br><br>* Barking<br><br>* Sniffing<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Coprolalia: uttering obscene or socially inappropriate words or phrases<br><br>* <u>Palilalia</u>: repeating words or phrases with increasing rapidity<br><br>* Echolalia: repeating vocalizations of others<br><br><br> |
| Motor <u>tics</u> | <br><br>* Facial grimacing<br><br>* Blinking<br><br>* Shoulder shrugging<br><br>* Head jerking<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Jumping<br><br>* Twisting the body<br><br>* Echopraxia: repeating movements of others<br><br><br> |

## Diagnosis

Primary <u>tic</u> disorders are <u>clinical diagnoses</u> confirmed with <u>DSM-5-TR</u> criteria. [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




### DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria for Tourette syndrome [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




The patient must meet all the following criteria:




* Onset < 18 years of age

* ≥ 2 motor <u>tics</u> and ≥ 1 vocal <u>tic</u>

* Symptoms persist for > 1 year (can wax and wane in frequency).

* Not explained by substance use or other medical conditions (see “Differential diagnoses”)





### DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria for persistent (chronic) motor or vocal tic disorder [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




The patient must meet all the following criteria:




* Onset < 18 years of age

* ≥ 1 motor or vocal <u>tics</u>

* Symptoms occur for > 1 year and can wax and wane in frequency.

* Criteria for <u>Tourette syndrome</u> are not met.

* Not explained by substance use or other medical conditions (see “Differential diagnoses”)





### DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria for provisional tic disorder [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




The patient must meet all the following criteria:




* Onset < 18 years of age

* ≥ 1 motor and/or vocal <u>tics</u>

* Symptoms occur for < 1 year.

* Criteria for other <u>tic</u> disorders are not met.

* Not explained by substance use or other medical conditions (see “Differential diagnoses”)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* Adult-onset tics [[3]](/library/3ucSIV0)[[4]](/library/RuclIV0)

* Onset of <u>tics</u> after the age of 18 years

* Primary <u>tics</u> (<u>idiopathic</u>): not explained by other medical conditions or substance use (e.g., <u>cocaine</u>); very rare

* Secondary <u>tics</u>: due to a medical condition (e.g., <u>brain lesions</u>, <u>brain injury</u>, <u>neurodegenerative disease</u>) or substance use; much more common

* <u>Stereotypic movement disorder</u>

* <u>Tardive dyskinesia</u>

* <u>Huntington disease</u>

* <u>Sydenham chorea</u> in <u>rheumatic fever</u>

* Spasmus nutans (<u>nodding spasm</u>)

* <u>Myoclonus</u>

* <u>Oromandibular dystonia</u>

* <u>Pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infections</u> (<u>PANDAS</u>)

* <u>Blepharospasm</u>

* <u>Hemifacial spasm</u>




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Management

In patients with chronic <u>tic</u> disorders, treatment is aimed at improving symptoms and quality of life. [[5]](/library/3VWS840)[[6]](/library/-KdDQI0)




### Approach [[5]](/library/3VWS840)[[6]](/library/-KdDQI0)




* All patients

* Educate patients, caregivers, and teachers on <u>tic</u> disorders.

* Assess for and treat comorbid conditions (e.g., <u>OCD</u>, <u>ADHD</u>).

* Determine the degree of functional impairment using a validated scale (e.g., Yale <u>Global</u> <u>Tic</u> Severity Scale-Revised).

* Patients with no functional impairment

* Consider <u>expectant management</u>.

* Refer for <u>CBIT</u>, if interested.

* Patients with functional impairment  [[2]](/library/06dejI0)[[6]](/library/-KdDQI0); 

* <u>Behavioral therapy</u> is the preferred initial treatment option.

* Pharmacological treatment or advanced treatments may be used depending on any of the following; consult a specialist:

* Degree of impairment

* Presence of comorbidities

* <u>Behavioral therapy</u> is ineffective or unavailable.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Tic</u> disorders can have a waxing and waning course; regularly assess the treatment regimens to determine the need for treatment escalation or tapering. [[5]](/library/3VWS840)




> [!WARNING]
> Closely monitor patients for <u>suicidal ideation</u> and start <u>management of suicidal behavior</u> if necessary. [[5]](/library/3VWS840)




### <u>Behavioral therapy</u> [[5]](/library/3VWS840)




* Comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics (<u>CBIT</u>)

* Indication: all patients with <u>tic</u> disorders and functional impairment

* Components [[2]](/library/06dejI0)

* <u>Habit reversal training</u>: to identify premonitory urges and train patients to suppress <u>tics</u>

* Functional assessment and intervention: to identify and change environmental situations that worsen <u>tics</u>

* Relaxation training (e.g., diaphragmatic breathing): to reduce <u>anxiety</u>

* Alternative options such as <u>exposure and response prevention</u> can be used if <u>CBIT</u> is not available.





### Pharmacological treatment [[5]](/library/3VWS840)




There is no consensus on a preferred drug; use <u>shared decision-making</u> and consider factors such as the risks and benefits of therapy and comorbid conditions.




* <u>Alpha-2 receptor agonists</u>;  (<u>off-label</u>): e.g., <u>clonidine</u>, <u>guanfacine</u>; can also be used for the <u>treatment of ADHD</u>

* <u>Dopamine antagonists</u>: e.g., <u>aripiprazole</u>, <u>haloperidol</u>, <u>risperidone</u> (<u>off-label</u>), <u>pimozide</u>

* Additional options with limited evidence include:

* <u>Topiramate</u> (<u>off-label</u>)

* <u>Vesicular monoamine transporter-2</u> inhibitors such as <u>tetrabenazine</u> (<u>off-label</u>)

* <u>Cannabis</u> (<u>off-label</u>)





### Advanced treatments [[5]](/library/3VWS840)




* <u>Botulinum toxin</u> injection: for focal motor <u>tics</u> or disabling vocal <u>tics</u> in adults and <u>adolescents</u>

* <u>Deep brain stimulation</u>: for severe <u>tics</u> (e.g., causing harm to the patient) or <u>tics</u> refractory to other treatment modalities

---

## Prognosis

* Symptoms improve during <u>adolescence</u>. [[7]](/library/Esd89r0)

* Most individuals experience no <u>tics</u> or only mild <u>tics</u> by early adulthood.
